# Wish World (Doctor Who)

"Wish World" is the seventh and penultimate episode of Series 15 (also designated Season 2 of the revival era) of the British science fiction television series *Doctor Who* [), ]. Premiering on May 24, 2025, it serves as the first part of a two-part season finale, with the second half titled "The Reality War" , . The episode is set within a fabricated alternate reality also named 'Wish World', which functions as the primary setting and antagonist of the narrative [), ]. Written by the show's current head writer, Russell T. Davies, and directed by Alex Pillai, "Wish World" marks the highly anticipated return of the Time Lord villain The Rani after a 38-year absence, portrayed by Archie Panjabi [), ]. The episode is notable for its ambitious thematic scope, weaving together satire of reactionary conservatism, critiques of media and nostalgia, and deep dives into the show's own mythology through the reintroduction of Omega , , . Airing simultaneously on BBC One in the United Kingdom and on the Disney+ streaming service globally, the episode represents a key installment in the modern revival era of the long-running series, produced under the BBC/Disney+ global broadcast partnership , .

## Production and Broadcast Details

The production of "Wish World" involved a core creative team responsible for shaping one of the most pivotal episodes of the 2025 season of *Doctor Who*. The episode was written by Russell T. Davies, who has served as the show's lead writer since its revival in 2005, bringing his distinctive voice and narrative ambition to the story , . Davies' writing credits include numerous acclaimed episodes across both the classic and revived eras, making his involvement a significant factor in the episode's development. The direction was handled by Alex Pillai, also credited as Alex Sanjiv Pillai in some sources, whose visual style contributed to the surreal and unsettling atmosphere of the fabricated reality , , . The episode was executive produced by a team including Russell T. Davies, Jane Tranter, Phil Collinson, Julie Gardner, Joel Collins, and Jo Pearce, reflecting the collaborative nature of producing the series under its current broadcasting model , . Music for the episode was composed by Murray Gold, whose score played a crucial role in establishing the dissonant and creeping unease characteristic of the "Wish World" setting , .

The episode was officially released on May 24, 2025, a date consistently reported across multiple sources [), , , ]. In the United Kingdom, it aired on BBC One at 6:50pm, following the 8am availability of the episode on the BBC iPlayer service . This dual-release strategy is standard for the modern revival of *Doctor Who*, catering to both traditional television viewers and the growing number of online streamers. Internationally, the episode launched simultaneously on the Disney+ platform, beginning at 3am Eastern Time / 12am Pacific Time, confirming its status as a product of the global streaming partnership between the BBC and Disney+ , . This distribution model ensures a synchronized worldwide viewing experience, a hallmark of the show's contemporary production and marketing efforts. The episode is officially categorized under the genres of science fiction, fantasy, adventure, and drama, aligning it with the established tone of the series while allowing for the exploration of more complex and mature themes .

As the seventh episode of the season, "Wish World" follows a sequence of stories that build upon each other, culminating in the season's conclusion. It precedes "The Interstellar Song Contest," which had a user rating of 7.1/10, and is followed by the final episode, "The Reality War," which received a notably lower rating of 4.5/10 . This placement is significant, as the episode is structured as the first part of a two-episode climax, designed to deliver major plot twists and unresolved cliffhangers that would be addressed in the subsequent installment , . The narrative deliberately withholds full closure, concentrating its payoffs for the finale and explaining why some critics and reviewers found its standalone impact somewhat diminished , . The episode's runtime is 45 minutes, presented as a single, self-contained telecast rather than split into separate segments [)]. Its TV-PG content rating suggests it contains material suitable for general audiences, though its thematic content delves into complex and sometimes disturbing subject matter . The production design, including the surreal suburban landscapes and the towering Bone Palace, was a key element of the episode, contributing to its high effect scores in audience polls , .

## Narrative and Plot Summary

The narrative of "Wish World" centers on the creation of a malevolent artificial reality by the renegade Time Lord, The Rani [)]. After a 38-year absence from the screen, The Rani returns in a new bi-generated form, portrayed by Archie Panjabi, having been generated from her previous incarnation, Mrs. Flood, played by Anita Dobson [), , ]. Her accomplice in this scheme is Conrad Clark, a manosphere conspiracy theorist podcaster introduced earlier in the season, who unknowingly becomes the unwitting architect of the reality through his subconscious desires [), , ]. To power this fabricated dimension, they utilize Desidirium, an infant deity from the Pantheon of Discord, who possesses the ability to grant wishes [), , ]. The result is "Wish World," a distorted and oppressive alternate Earth designed to conform to Conrad's reactionary fantasies [), ].

The Doctor, portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, and his companion Belinda Chandra, played by Varada Sethu, are captured and transported into this false reality , . Within "Wish World," their identities are twisted and reimagined. The Doctor is cast as "John Smith," a mundane employee for a fictionalized version of UNIT called the "Unified National Insurance Team" . Belinda is recast as his domestic partner and mother to a daughter named Poppy, a child she had not previously had , . Their friends are also trapped in altered roles; Mel Bush appears as Belinda's neighbor, Susan Triad works as a tea-lady for UNIT, and Ruby Sunday finds herself as a skeptical observer of the perfect world , . Conrad himself functions as the reality's authoritarian narrator, broadcasting from a control center known as the Bone Palace, a massive spider-like structure housing fossilized creatures , . His constant broadcasts promise beautiful weather while he visibly strains under the effort of maintaining the illusion .

The core of the plot is revealed mid-episode: "Wish World" is not an end in itself but a carefully constructed trap designed by The Rani . Her ultimate goal is to harness collective doubt, particularly the Doctor's inherent capacity for skepticism, to tear open the fabric of reality , . By exploiting the Doctor's curiosity and intelligence, she intends to create gateways to the Underverse—a mysterious dimension beneath reality—to locate Omega, an ancient and powerful Time Lord figure imprisoned there [), ]. The plan involves forming an "Unholy Trinity" with Conrad and Omega, a cosmic threat that would enable The Rani to access all Time Lord knowledge [), , ]. The Doctor's presence is the catalyst; his very nature as someone who questions everything makes him the perfect target to destabilize the fabricated world .

The climax of the episode sees the Doctor begin to unravel the truth of their situation. He realizes that doubt is the key to breaking the spell. In a pivotal moment, he publicly asserts his queerness, directly confronting the homophobic and heteronormative ideals enforced by Conrad's reality . This act of personal truth shatters the illusion, causing the oppressive suburban facade to crumble and freeing his companions from their stifling roles . However, the victory is short-lived. The Doctor's defiance accelerates the collapse of "Wish World." As the reality disintegrates on May 25, 2025, the planet Earth itself begins to sink into the Underverse [), ]. The episode concludes on a dramatic cliffhanger: the Doctor, holding his young daughter Poppy, shouts, "I have a daughter! Poppy is real!" before falling into the abyss with his companion Belinda, who has been physically isolated in a soundproofed box during the chaos , , . The Ranis, watching from their palace, toast at midnight, signaling their success in luring the Doctor to the brink of destruction .

## Thematic Analysis and Social Commentary

Beyond its intricate science fiction plot, "Wish World" is a deeply thematically rich episode that engages in sharp social and political commentary, primarily through satire and metafiction. The central theme is a direct and unflinching critique of reactionary conservatism, heteronormativity, pronatalism, and ableism [), , , ]. The fabricated reality of "Wish World" is meticulously constructed to represent a chilling vision of a society built on these toxic ideals, manifesting as a pastel-colored, surreal suburban landscape that evokes the domestic ideal of the 1950s , , . This aesthetic is explicitly linked to the "Stepford Wives" trope, where women are confined to kitchens and men wear bowler hats, creating a surface-level perfection that masks profound oppression , . The episode further satirizes specific contemporary phenomena, including "tradwife" aesthetics and the ideologies prevalent in the manosphere, which are embodied by the character of Conrad Clark , . The world criminalizes non-conformity, marginalizing disabled people and drag queens, presenting these groups as "castoffs" to be erased from the narrative , , . By placing the Doctor, a queer icon, at the center of this homophobic reality, the episode uses its protagonist's identity as a weapon to dismantle the oppressive system from within .

Another major theme is the power of stories, media, and nostalgia to warp reality and belief. "Wish World" operates on a powerful metafictional level, exploring how narratives—especially those consumed by children—are absorbed and internalized, becoming the very foundation of a person's worldview . The concept that "these things do grow in legend. They become the legend," articulated by Russell T. Davies, encapsulates this idea, reflecting on the process of mythmaking within the *Doctor Who* canon itself . The episode’s portrayal of the Doctor as a fictional character within a manufactured "Doctor Who" franchise narrated by Conrad is a direct jab at the blurring line between entertainment and perceived reality , . This self-referential critique extends to real-world media, using intertextual references to anchor its satire in familiar cultural touchstones . The show draws explicit parallels to *WandaVision* for its exploration of a reality-warping sitcom, and includes jabs at *Harry Potter*, *Star Wars*, *Aliens*, and *Alice in Wonderland* to underscore its themes of media distortion and the dangers of uncritical wish-fulfillment fantasy , , . This strategy frames the episode as a warning against the uncritical consumption of nostalgic media constructs that often mask underlying authoritarian fantasies .

The episode also delves into the psychological mechanics of belief and the fragility of constructed realities. The core mechanism driving the plot is that doubt is the only force capable of collapsing "Wish World" , . The Doctor's inherent nature as a being defined by curiosity and skepticism makes him uniquely suited to see through the illusion. The visual motif of a shattering mug, symbolizing the Doctor's growing doubt, acts as a catalyst for the apocalypse, demonstrating that these authoritarian fantasies are fundamentally unsustainable and built on a foundation of fragile lies , . The narrative suggests that the greatest threat to such systems is not brute force, but the quiet, persistent act of questioning. Furthermore, the episode critiques the dynamics of "thought policing" and authoritarian fantasy, showing how a society that suppresses doubt and enforces a singular narrative ultimately destroys itself , . The ending, where the Doctor's assertion of his true identity causes the entire reality to implode, serves as a potent metaphor for the power of truth and authenticity to liberate individuals from oppressive systems of thought . The episode thus positions personal identity not just as a source of strength, but as a fundamental force capable of dismantling even the most elaborate ideological constructs.

## Character Introductions and Returns

"Wish World" features a mix of returning fan-favorite characters and the introduction of new ones, all integral to advancing the episode's complex plot and deepening its engagement with *Doctor Who*'s rich history. The most significant return is that of The Rani, a recurring Time Lord villain who last appeared on-screen in 1987's "Time and the Rani" [), ]. Portrayed by Archie Panjabi, this new incarnation is the result of a bi-generation process from Mrs. Flood (Anita Dobson), a character who debuted in the preceding episode, "The Interstellar Song Contest" , . This bi-generation allows for a unique dynamic, with both Panjabi and Dobson appearing as different incarnations of the same character, enabling intra-Rani betrayal and adding a layer of complexity to the villain's schemes , . The Rani is depicted as a ruthless and amoral biochemist who experiments on other species, and her motivation in this episode is grandiose: she aims to harness collective doubt to breach reality and free Omega, thereby gaining all Time Lord knowledge , . Panjabi's performance was widely praised, with many critics calling it "the best Rani episode of all time" , .

The central protagonist, the Fourteenth Doctor, is portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, who continues in the role following the events of the 2024 Christmas Special, "Joy to the World" . In "Wish World," Gatwa's Doctor is trapped in the persona of John Smith, a UNIT employee, which serves to highlight his frustration and alienation . His journey throughout the episode is one of regaining his true identity and using his intellect and empathy to expose the falsehood of "Wish World." Another key character is Belinda Chandra, the Doctor's companion played by Varada Sethu . While Belinda is a central character in the episode, her narrative arc has been noted by critics for significant sidelining. She is largely passive, forced into the role of a domestic housewife, and her agency is further diminished when she is physically isolated in a soundproofed box during the climax of the season finale, a decision described by some reviewers as "bewildering" . This treatment has sparked debate about the handling of female companions in the series' recent seasons.

The primary antagonist of the fabricated reality is Conrad Clark, played by Jonah Hauer-King , . Introduced in the episode "Lucky Day," Conrad is established as a misogynistic former boyfriend of Ruby Sunday and a manosphere conspiracy theorist podcaster , . Within "Wish World," he serves as the subconscious source of the reality's reactionary ideology and its authoritarian narrator, promising a perfect world while struggling to maintain the illusion , . His character represents the real-world danger of online ideologies that seek to impose a narrow, exclusionary vision of society onto reality. Other notable characters include Mel Bush, played by Bonnie Langford, who appears as Belinda's neighbor and provides a crucial link to the past, and Susan Triad, portrayed by Susan Twist, who takes on the role of a UNIT tea-lady , . The episode also makes several callbacks to classic *Doctor Who* lore. The audio of Stephen Thorne, who originally played Omega, is used, reintroducing the foundational Time Lord villain to the modern series [), ]. Additionally, vintage clips of Kate O'Mara, the original actress to portray The Rani, are featured, reinforcing the character's canonical status and providing a nostalgic touch for long-time fans , .

## Critical Reception and Audience Response

The reception of "Wish World" was sharply polarized, reflecting a significant divide between critics and audiences, and among different factions of the reviewer community. On one end of the spectrum, several outlets offered overwhelmingly positive reviews, praising the episode's bold ambition and successful execution of its complex themes. Film Stories, for instance, published a spoiler-filled review immediately following the episode's premiere, declaring it "the best Rani episode in the history of the series" , . This sentiment was echoed in other analyses that commended the episode's sophisticated satire of reactionary ideology, its effective use of intertextuality, and the powerful performances, particularly that of Archie Panjabi as The Rani , . These reviewers framed the episode as a thematic culmination of ideas introduced throughout the season, lauding its willingness to engage with timely and contentious subjects . The visual design of the surreal, Tim Burton-esque suburbia and the giant bone creatures were also frequently highlighted as standout achievements, contributing to a high average user rating for effects on IMDb , .

Conversely, a segment of the critical community delivered scathing reviews, finding the episode to be a failure of execution despite its thematic ambitions. IGN Movies provided one of the harshest critiques, awarding the episode a dismal 3 out of 10 . The review accused the episode of embodying "the worst instincts of Doctor Who’s Disney era," describing it as "glossy, confused, and screaming for attention" . Critics leveled charges of "shameless lore dumping" and "shallow storytelling," suggesting that the heavy exposition and dense mythology undermined the narrative's clarity and emotional impact , . This negative perspective viewed the episode's structural choices, such as its slow pacing and deliberate lack of narrative closure, not as a feature of serialized storytelling but as a flaw in its standalone presentation , . The contrast between this review and others within the same season is stark; for example, "The Interstellar Song Contest" received an 8/10, and "Lux" received a 9/10, positioning "Wish World" as a critical outlier .

Audience reception, as measured by platforms like IMDb, presents a more moderate picture. The episode holds an average user rating of 7.1 out of 10, based on 53 votes . This indicates that while it was divisive, it was not universally panned by the general viewer base. The breakdown of ratings reveals interesting insights: the technical aspects of the episode were well-received, with Effects scoring a strong 8.2/10 and Acting receiving a respectable 7.7/10 . However, the Plot received a much lower mark of 6.9/10, suggesting that while the visuals and performances were appreciated, the narrative structure and pacing were points of contention for many viewers . A crucial piece of data from the audience poll is that 100% of the 50 raters indicated that prior viewing of preceding episodes was necessary to fully understand and appreciate "Wish World" . This underscores the episode's heavy reliance on its serialized context and explains why its reception is so difficult to evaluate in isolation. Common criticisms from audiences and critics alike included the constrained character development for Ncuti Gatwa's Doctor, who had only 17 episodes in the season, and the unresolved cliffhangers that felt unsatisfying without the benefit of the next episode's resolution . The controversial narrative treatment of the companion Belinda Chandra was another frequent point of discussion, with some viewers expressing confusion or dissatisfaction with her diminished role .

## Significance and Legacy within Doctor Who

"Wish World" holds considerable significance within the broader *Doctor Who* canon due to its role in reintroducing major characters, advancing a large-scale season-long narrative, and engaging with the series' own history in a meaningful way. As the first part of a two-part season finale, the episode functions as a narrative culmination, tying together various plot threads from the preceding twenty episodes of the revival era . Its placement elevates the stakes dramatically, moving the series beyond episodic adventures into a more serialized and epic confrontation. The episode's importance is cemented by the return of The Rani, a villain with a deep legacy dating back to the 1980s, and the reintroduction of Omega, a foundational figure from the show's earliest years, specifically the 1972–73 serial "The Three Doctors" [), , ]. The use of archived audio for Omega connects the modern revival directly to its classic roots, a technique that validates the character's historical importance and signals to the audience that the stakes are now cosmological in scale [)]. The formation of an "Unholy Trinity" involving Conrad, The Rani, and Omega sets up a formidable threat for the remainder of the season, potentially leading to a universe-altering conflict that could reshape Gallifreyan lore [), ].

The episode also contributes significantly to the ongoing character arcs of the current Doctor and his companions. For the Fourteenth Doctor, portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, "Wish World" presents a unique psychological challenge, forcing him to confront a reality that attacks his very sense of identity and purpose . His journey to reclaim his name and his courage is a central pillar of the narrative, showcasing his resilience in the face of existential manipulation. For the companion Belinda Chandra, the episode marks a turning point, albeit a controversial one. The fabrication of a family unit with the Doctor, including a daughter named Poppy, introduces a new layer of emotional vulnerability and stakes , . The confirmation that Poppy is "very real" serves as a crucial emotional payoff, yet the manner in which her existence is threatened and the subsequent treatment of Belinda have been interpreted by some as a problematic narrative choice, potentially undermining her character's agency , . This ambiguity leaves her future role in the series uncertain and opens up a dialogue about the representation and empowerment of female companions.

In conclusion, "Wish World" stands as a landmark episode in the modern revival of *Doctor Who*, defined by its high-risk, high-reward approach to storytelling. It successfully leverages the serialized format of the Disney+ season to deliver a narrative that is both a thrilling sci-fi adventure and a potent piece of social satire. While its reception has been mixed, its impact is undeniable. The episode solidifies the return of one of the Doctor's most enduring enemies, reintroduces a cornerstone of Time Lord mythology, and pushes the series towards a more serialized and mythologically dense future. Its legacy will likely be defined by this ambitious fusion of genre spectacle and topical commentary, ensuring it remains a memorable and debated chapter in the long history of the programme. Whether viewed as a masterpiece of modern television or a flawed but audacious experiment, "Wish World" cements its place as a pivotal moment in the evolution of *Doctor Who* in the 21st century.

Conrad Clark is a manosphere conspiracy theorist podcaster.
Conrad Clark was introduced earlier in the season.
Conrad Clark unknowingly becomes the unwitting architect of the reality through his subconscious desires.
To power the fabricated dimension, The Rani and Conrad Clark utilize Desidirium.
Desidirium is an infant deity from the Pantheon of Discord.
Desidirium possesses the ability to grant wishes.
The result of the scheme is 'Wish World'.
'Wish World' is a distorted and oppressive alternate Earth.
'Wish World' is designed to conform to Conrad's reactionary fantasies.
The Doctor is portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa.
The Doctor and his companion Belinda Chandra are captured and transported into the false reality of 'Wish World'.
Belinda Chandra is played by Varada Sethu.
Within 'Wish World,' The Doctor is cast as 'John Smith'.
'John Smith' is a mundane employee for a fictionalized version of UNIT called the 'Unified National Insurance Team'.
Belinda is recast as The Doctor's domestic partner within 'Wish World'.
Belinda is recast as mother to a daughter named Poppy within 'Wish World'.
Belinda had not previously had a child named Poppy.
The Doctor and Belinda's friends are also trapped in altered roles within 'Wish World'.
Mel Bush appears as Belinda's neighbor within 'Wish World'.
Susan Triad works as a tea-lady for UNIT within 'Wish World'.
Ruby Sunday finds herself as a skeptical observer of the perfect world within 'Wish World'.
Conrad Clark functions as 'Wish World's authoritarian narrator.
Conrad Clark broadcasts from a control center known as the Bone Palace.
The Bone Palace is a massive spider-like structure housing fossilized creatures.
Conrad Clark's constant broadcasts promise beautiful weather within 'Wish World'.
Conrad Clark visibly strains under the effort of maintaining the illusion of 'Wish World'.
The core of the plot of 'Wish World' is revealed mid-episode.
'Wish World' is not an end in itself.
'Wish World' is a carefully constructed trap designed by The Rani.
The Rani's ultimate goal is to harness collective doubt to tear open the fabric of reality.
The Rani's ultimate goal particularly targets the Doctor's inherent capacity for skepticism.
By exploiting the Doctor's curiosity and intelligence, The Rani intends to create gateways to the Underverse.
The Underverse is a mysterious dimension beneath reality.
The Rani intends to locate Omega, an ancient and powerful Time Lord figure imprisoned in the Underverse.
The Rani's plan involves forming an 'Unholy Trinity' with Conrad and Omega.
The 'Unholy Trinity' with Conrad and Omega is a cosmic threat.
The 'Unholy Trinity' would enable The Rani to access all Time Lord knowledge.
The Doctor's presence is the catalyst for The Rani's plan.
The Doctor's very nature as someone who questions everything makes him the perfect target to destabilize the fabricated world.
The climax of the episode sees the Doctor begin to unravel the truth of their situation.
The Doctor realizes that doubt is the key to breaking the spell of 'Wish World'.
In a pivotal moment, the Doctor publicly asserts his queerness, directly confronting the homophobic and heteronormative ideals enforced by Conrad's reality.
The Doctor's act of personal truth shatters the illusion of 'Wish World'.
The Doctor's act of personal truth causes the oppressive suburban facade to crumble.
The Doctor's act of personal truth frees his companions from their stifling roles.
The victory of the Doctor is short-lived.
The Doctor's defiance accelerates the collapse of 'Wish World'.
As the reality disintegrates on May 25, 2025, the planet Earth itself begins to sink into the Underverse.
The episode concludes on a dramatic cliffhanger.
The Doctor, holding his young daughter Poppy, shouts, 'I have a daughter! Poppy is real!' before falling into the abyss with his companion Belinda.
Belinda has been physically isolated in a soundproofed box during the chaos.
The Ranis, watching from their palace, toast at midnight, signaling their success in luring the Doctor to the brink of destruction.
'Wish World' is a deeply thematically rich episode that engages in sharp social and political commentary, primarily through satire and metafiction.
The central theme of 'Wish World' is a direct and unflinching critique of reactionary conservatism, heteronormativity, pronatalism, and ableism.
The fabricated reality of 'Wish World' is meticulously constructed to represent a chilling vision of a society built on toxic ideals.
The fabricated reality of 'Wish World' manifests as a pastel-colored, surreal suburban landscape that evokes the domestic ideal of the 1950s.
This aesthetic is explicitly linked to the 'Stepford Wives' trope.
In the 'Stepford Wives' trope, women are confined to kitchens and men wear bowler hats, creating a surface-level perfection that masks profound oppression.
The episode further satirizes specific contemporary phenomena, including 'tradwife' aesthetics and the ideologies prevalent in the manosphere.
The ideologies prevalent in the manosphere are embodied by the character of Conrad Clark.
The world of 'Wish World' criminalizes non-conformity.
The world of 'Wish World' marginalizes disabled people and drag queens.
Disabled people and drag queens are presented as 'castoffs' to be erased from the narrative in 'Wish World'.
By placing the Doctor, a queer icon, at the center of this homophobic reality, the episode uses its protagonist's identity as a weapon to dismantle the oppressive system from within.
Another major theme of 'Wish World' is the power of stories, media, and nostalgia to warp reality and belief.
'Wish World' operates on a powerful metafictional level, exploring how narratives are absorbed and internalized, becoming the very foundation of a person's worldview.
The concept that 'these things do grow in legend. They become the legend,' articulated by Russell T. Davies, encapsulates the idea of mythmaking within the *Doctor Who* canon itself.

The episode's portrayal of the Doctor as a fictional character within a manufactured 'Doctor Who' franchise narrated by Conrad is a direct jab at the blurring line between entertainment and perceived reality.
This self-referential critique extends to real-world media, using intertextual references to anchor its satire in familiar cultural touchstones.
The show draws explicit parallels to *WandaVision* for its exploration of a reality-warping sitcom.
'Wish World' includes jabs at *Harry Potter*, *Star Wars*, *Aliens*, and *Alice in Wonderland* to underscore its themes of media distortion and the dangers of uncritical wish-fulfillment fantasy.
This strategy frames the episode as a warning against the uncritical consumption of nostalgic media constructs that often mask underlying authoritarian fantasies.
The episode also delves into the psychological mechanics of belief and the fragility of constructed realities.
The core mechanism driving the plot of 'Wish World' is that doubt is the only force capable of collapsing it.
The Doctor's inherent nature as a being defined by curiosity and skepticism makes him uniquely suited to see through the illusion.
The visual motif of a shattering mug, symbolizing the Doctor's growing doubt, acts as a catalyst for the apocalypse.
The shattering mug demonstrates that these authoritarian fantasies are fundamentally unsustainable and built on a foundation of fragile lies.
The narrative suggests that the greatest threat to such systems is not brute force, but the quiet, persistent act of questioning.
The episode critiques the dynamics of 'thought policing' and authoritarian fantasy.
The episode shows how a society that suppresses doubt and enforces a singular narrative ultimately destroys itself.

The ending, where the Doctor's assertion of his true identity causes the entire reality to implode, serves as a potent metaphor for the power of truth and authenticity to liberate individuals from oppressive systems of thought.
The episode thus positions personal identity not just as a source of strength, but as a fundamental force capable of dismantling even the most elaborate ideological constructs.
'Wish World' features a mix of returning fan-favorite characters and the introduction of new ones.
All characters in 'Wish World' are integral to advancing the episode's complex plot and deepening its engagement with *Doctor Who*'s rich history.
The most significant return in 'Wish World' is that of The Rani, a recurring Time Lord villain who last appeared on-screen in 1987's 'Time and the Rani'.
The Rani is portrayed by Archie Panjabi in 'Wish World'.
This new incarnation of The Rani is the result of a bi-generation process from Mrs. Flood (Anita Dobson).
Mrs. Flood debuted in the preceding episode, 'The Interstellar Song Contest'.
This bi-generation allows for a unique dynamic, with both Panjabi and Dobson appearing as different incarnations of the same character.
The bi-generation enables intra-Rani betrayal and adds a layer of complexity to the villain's schemes.
The Rani is depicted as a ruthless and amoral biochemist who experiments on other species.
The Rani's motivation in 'Wish World' is grandiose: she aims to harness collective doubt to breach reality and free Omega, thereby gaining all Time Lord knowledge.
Panjabi's performance as The Rani was widely praised.
Many critics called Panjabi's performance as The Rani 'the best Rani episode of all time'.
The central protagonist, the Fourteenth Doctor, is portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa.
Ncuti Gatwa continues in the role of the Fourteenth Doctor following the events of the 2024 Christmas Special, 'Joy to the World'.
In 'Wish World,' Gatwa's Doctor is trapped in the persona of John Smith, a UNIT employee.

_[Doctor Who](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho")_ [recap index](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho")  
**Fifteenth Doctor Era**  
**Season 2:** [CS](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2024CSJoyToTheWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2024CSJoyToTheWorld") | [1](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution") | [2](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux") | [3](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E3TheWell "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E3TheWell") | [4](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay") | [5](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine") | [6](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest") | **7** | [8](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar")  
**[<<< Season 1](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2023CSTheChurchOnRubyRoad "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2023CSTheChurchOnRubyRoad")**

Wish World
----------

![Image 1: Doctor Who S41 E7 "Wish World" Recap](https://mediaproxy.tvtropes.org/width/1200/https://static.tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pub/images/wishworldtitlecard.jpeg)

Once upon a time, there was a Doctor and a Time Lady...

Written by [Russell T Davies](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RussellTDavies")  
Directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai  
**Air date:** 24 May 2025  
**Part 1 of 2**

_"I ask you, how can_ anyone _doubt this glorious world we live in?"_

— **John Smith**

[The One](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/JustForFun/TheOneWith "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/JustForFun/TheOneWith") [Who Is Lost...](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Pun "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Pun") _**[has](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E1TheThreeDoctors "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E1TheThreeDoctors") [been](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E1ArcOfInfinity "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E1ArcOfInfinity") [found.](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack")**_ Also known as the one where [tables don't do that](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcWords "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcWords").

* * *

Tropes. Don't. Do. That.
------------------------

*   [Actor Allusion](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ActorAllusion "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ActorAllusion"): The episode resonates strongly with [Ncuti Gatwa](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/NcutiGatwa "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/NcutiGatwa")'s role in _[Barbie](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Film/Barbie2023 "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Film/Barbie2023")_, about a seemingly perfect world that actually hides a dark undercurrent of prejudice, and can be thrown into chaos simply by someone questioning the nature of it.
*   [Africa Is a Country](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AfricaIsACountry "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AfricaIsACountry"): During his broadcast, Conrad "reports" on the weather in [France](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/France "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/France"), [Venezuela](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/Venezuela "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/Venezuela"), [New Zealand](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/NewZealand "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/NewZealand"), and, for whatever reason, Africa.
*   [Apocalypse How](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypseHow "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypseHow"): Once all the doubts of the people living in Conrad's wish society, especially those of the Doctor, reach critical mass, pits of purple energy (implied to be gateways to the Underverse) start to open across Earth, causing everything atop them to fall in.
*   [Arc Number](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcNumber "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcNumber"): It's not featured very heavily, but with the wish world being powered by the seventh son of a seventh son of a seventh son, it's notable that the Doubt Police insignia is a crown made of 7s.
*   [Arc Words](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcWords "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcWords"): Doubt. Many posters in Conrad's reality warn against it, and it's what powers the Ranis' portal into the Underverse.
*   [Back from the Dead](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BackFromTheDead "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BackFromTheDead"): Despite his last on-screen appearance ending with him looking pretty comprehensively dead, what with dying and dissolving into dust, Omega returns (though the Doctor did say at the time he wasn't sure Omega was actually dead).
*   [Batman Gambit](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BatmanGambit "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BatmanGambit"): Turns out that all the doubts that everyone on Earth is having, especially the Doctor, aren't just [A Glitch in the Matrix](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix")—they're an intentional part of the Ranis' plot. With the help of the Vindicator and Desidirium's power, they gather enough energy to allow Omega to be freed from the Underverse.
*   [Bob from Accounting](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BobFromAccounting "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BobFromAccounting"): When John Smith advises Ibrahim on how to ask out Kate Stewart:**John:** I’ve heard she loves Chinese food. **Debra in accounts** says Kate swears by it. Loves it.
    
*   [Big Bad](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BigBad "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BigBad"): The Rani uses Desidirium and Conrad to create a fake reality in order to destroy Earth so she can release Omega.
*   [Bookends](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BookEnds "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BookEnds"): "[The Robot Revolution](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution")" began this series with the planet Missbelindachandra, a nightmare world shaped by the whims of Alan, a misogynist ex-boyfriend of the 15th Doctor’s companion-to-be, who was given power over the robots by a boot paradox. "Wish World" begins the finale with the titular Wish World, another nightmare world shaped by the whims of Conrad, a misogynist former boyfriend of the 15th Doctor’s former companion, who was given the power of Desidirium through a similar paradox. From an aesthetic perspective, Missbelindachandra has a 1950s sci-fi motif, while Wish World has a 1960s motif, despite both stories taking place in 2025.
*   [Briar Patching](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BriarPatching "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BriarPatching"): The Ranis are well aware that people will doubt Conrad's reality, and they encourage this through constant warnings not to. The more this occurs, the closer they get to opening a portal into the Underverse.
*   [Brick Joke](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BrickJoke "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BrickJoke"): Back in ["Empire of Death"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath"), Susan Triad offered to join UNIT, even if it was just to make tea, with Colonel Ibrahim's reaction suggesting he'd rather she didn't. In Conrad's world, she is UNIT's tea-lady, but the Doctor never gets around to drinking any thanks to a slip.
*   [The Bus Came Back](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBusCameBack"):
    *   John and Belinda's baby is Poppy the Space Baby... who has somehow wound up on Earth in the 21st century.
    *   Mel returns, as "John" and Belinda's next-door neighbour.
    *   The Rani's plan is to free Omega from beneath the Underverse.
    *   Rogue makes a brief reappearance after having last been seen in [his titular episode](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue"), still stuck in the dimension he was sent to at the end of that episode.
    *   Susan Triad returns as a tea maid in the wish version of UNIT.
*   [Call-Back](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallBack "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CallBack"):
    *   The Rani being able to forcibly transform people into various plants and animals is reminiscent of her infamous [tree mines](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Transflormation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Transflormation") from "[The Mark of the Rani](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS22E3TheMarkOfTheRani "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS22E3TheMarkOfTheRani")".
    *   The Doctor takes up the human moniker of [John](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS5E7TheWheelInSpace "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS5E7TheWheelInSpace") [Smith](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E3SchoolReunion "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E3SchoolReunion") [once](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E8HumanNature "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E8HumanNature") [again.](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E9TheFamilyofBlood "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E9TheFamilyofBlood")
    *   Ruby's experiences in "[73 Yards](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards")" seem to have given her a limited resistance to Conrad's Wish World.
    *   Susan Triad wears her tea lady outfit from "[The Devil's Chord](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E2TheDevilsChord "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E2TheDevilsChord")".
*   [The Cameo](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheCameo "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheCameo"): Susan Foreman and [Jonathan Groff's Rogue](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue") both return briefly on John Smith's television, as does popular Whovian Youtube personality Tharries as one of Shirley's group.
*   [Canon Welding](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CanonWelding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CanonWelding"): One of the stock clips used to portray Kate O’Mara’s incarnation of the Rani is from the long-held-as-non-canon [“Dimensions in Time”](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho30thASDimensionsInTime "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho30thASDimensionsInTime").
*   [Cliffhanger](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CliffHanger "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CliffHanger"): As May 24 begins, the entirety of Earth [starts to sink into the Underverse](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypseHow "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ApocalypseHow"), _seemingly_ spelling certain doom for everyone on Earth (including Ruby Sunday and Poppy) and bringing about the return of [Omega](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OmnicidalManiac "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OmnicidalManiac"). Belinda is trapped outside the Threshold, the Doctor is about to fall face-first into the Underverse, and the Ranis [raise a toast](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/VillainRaisesAToast "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/VillainRaisesAToast") as the clock strikes midnight. It's "seemingly" because it's not clear if humanity is _actually_ going to die — they may just be "relocated" to the Underverse the way that Rogue was to his current dimension, though the Ranis are assuming the former. And where _are_ Rogue and Susan anyway? And what happened to the TARDIS? And why does the Doctor make a point of shouting "I have a daughter! Poppy is real!" rather than trying to escape?
*   [Continuity Nod](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ContinuityNod "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ContinuityNod"):
    *   On realising things are messed up, Belinda runs off to scream, much in the same way the Doctor screamed at the sight of everything dying in ["Empire of Death"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath").
    *   Way back in his first appearance, Omega complained that the Time Lords revered him as a hero when he would rather have been a _god_. Looks like he's managed to get his wish.
    *   The Rani suggests that she and the Doctor may have a romantic history; in the [Big Finish](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/AudioPlay/BigFinishDoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/AudioPlay/BigFinishDoctorWho") audio story "The Bekdel Test" (part of Series 5 of _[The Diary of River Song](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/TheDiaryOfRiverSong "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/TheDiaryOfRiverSong")_), River Song tells Missy that she suspects the Doctor had crushes on both the Rani and the Master when they were at the academy together.
*   [Cosy Catastrophe](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CosyCatastrophe "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CosyCatastrophe"): To an extent. Shirley notes that she has no money for the state-of-the-art wheelchair she still possesses and feels perfectly fine despite her spinal bifida going untreated; the same presumably applies to everyone else in the encampment. [False Utopia](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FalseUtopia "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FalseUtopia") it might be, but it's softened by the necessities of life no longer being all that necessary.
*   [Crapsaccharine World](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CrapsaccharineWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CrapsaccharineWorld"): With an unusual twist: sustaining the [False Utopia](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FalseUtopia "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FalseUtopia") is not the antagonist's end goal, getting people to doubt it is the entire point.
*   [Cryptic Background Reference](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CrypticBackgroundReference "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CrypticBackgroundReference"): Trying to jog the Doctor's memories, the new Rani recalls their dance during the Siege of Persephone.
*   [Deliberate Values Dissonance](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DeliberateValuesDissonance "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DeliberateValuesDissonance"):
    *   Another part of Conrad's world. Men like women and vice-versa, and that's _all_ that's allowed. "John Smith" making an innocuous remark about Ibrahim being a good-looking guy gets him a filthy look and an intense interrogation.
    *   Women are expected to be loyal wives and mothers and nothing else, and while some women like Kate Stewart are still shown holding down authoritative positions, the way Kate is depicted makes her look like an old spinster, and John Smith and Ibrahim discuss how marrying Kate would be "saving" her from having to work. Mel, likewise, because she is a single senior woman with no family, is relegated to spending her days in silent contemplation, instead of being able to do _anything_ with her free time.
    *   The disabled population are looked down upon so much that they are all homeless and practically invisible to everyone else. Ruby even apologises to Shirley for _talking_ to her once she notices Shirley is disabled, noting how she's not supposed to. While this is assumed to be an effect of Conrad himself having so little regard for people like Shirley that they're not given any roles in his wished world and have to live in the margins, it's also not very far removed from what this sort of era was like for the poor and disabled.
    *   During his broadcast, Conrad "reports" on the weather in [France](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/France "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/France"), [Venezuela](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/Venezuela "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/Venezuela"), [New Zealand](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/NewZealand "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/NewZealand"), and Africa—this, at a time when people have been encouraged to see the continent not as a country, but a collection of nations. It's even more egregious given that he also mentions Missouri, a subnational entity of the United States.
*   [Does This Remind You of Anything?](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DoesThisRemindYouOfAnything "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DoesThisRemindYouOfAnything"): The Doctor/John Smith's confrontation with Belinda over how tables [really shouldn't do that](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix"), a realisation prompted by a man he 'really liked' causes Belinda to tearfully report him for 'doubt'. Since the Fifteenth Doctor is to all intents and purposes a gay man, it inevitably plays out like a woman learning that she's [The Beard](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBeard "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheBeard").
*   [Elephant in the Living Room](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ElephantInTheLivingRoom "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ElephantInTheLivingRoom"): Whenever a "slip" happens, everyone tries to ignore their doubts and brush past things like it never happened.
*   [Enforced Technology Levels](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EnforcedTechnologyLevels "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EnforcedTechnologyLevels"): As part of Conrad's wish world, there's no tech more advanced than anything past the 1960s, so no mobile phones, no computers, and no tablets. Shirley's still got her old UNIT tablet because it slipped through the cracks, but has no real memory of what it is.
*   [Even Evil Has Standards](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EvenEvilHasStandards "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EvenEvilHasStandards"): For all the bigoted and traditionalist views Conrad holds that are reflected in his wished world, the fact that dark-skinned people like "John Smith" and Belinda are treated the same as everyone else suggests that he's not a racist to any significant degree (although in one of his broadcasts he does make the common Eurocentric blunder of referring to Africa as if it's all one place).
*   [Evil Is Petty](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EvilIsPetty "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EvilIsPetty"):
    *   While taking Desidirium, the Rani turns his mother into violet petals, his brothers into ducks, and his father into an owl, all for no apparent reason besides trying out the baby's powers.
    *   It probably isn't a coincidence that in a world made by Conrad, Kate Stewart is a dowdy spinster.
*   [Felony Misdemeanour](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FelonyMisdemeanour "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FelonyMisdemeanour"): Doubts of any kind—as well as, apparently, not trusting Conrad—are supposed to warrant a visit from the police.
*   [Female Misogynist](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FemaleMisogynist "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FemaleMisogynist"): The Rani and Ms. Flood seemingly have no problems with the [Stay in the Kitchen](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StayInTheKitchen "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StayInTheKitchen") attitude of [Conrad](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheDragon "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheDragon").
*   [Flashback-Montage Realization](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FlashbackMontageRealization "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FlashbackMontageRealization"): As the Rani explains the Vindicator's true purpose, scenes where it's been used are played.
*   [Forced Transformation](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ForcedTransformation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ForcedTransformation"): Whilst taking Desidirium, the Rani turns his mother into violets, his brothers into ducks, and his father into an owl.
*   [Genre Savvy](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GenreSavvy "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GenreSavvy"):
    *   The Rani, knowing the Doctor would try to stop her once [having served his purpose in her plan](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouHaveOutlivedYourUsefulness "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouHaveOutlivedYourUsefulness"), detonates the balcony edge of her bone temple after placing the Doctor on it, sending him crashing into the [World-Wrecking Wave](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldWreckingWave "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldWreckingWave") below.
    *   Her entire plan shows an awareness of the fault in classic [Lotus-Eater Machine](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LotusEaterMachine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LotusEaterMachine") plots: that there will always be those who don't fall for the false reality and question its inconsistencies. She weaponises this to create a false reality so powerful that when it inevitably breaks (particularly by the hands of a being as powerful as the Doctor), the cataclysm is enough to shatter reality itself.
    *   She also says explicitly that she knows better than to let the Doctor into the central room with Conrad and Desidirium, and just makes the door transparent so that he can see inside for a moment.
*   [A Glitch in the Matrix](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGlitchInTheMatrix"): Belinda, her mum and grandmother are talking about Poppy's birth, only to suddenly realise they don't recall _anything_ about the event.
*   [A God Am I](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGodAmI "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGodAmI"): Conrad uses the power of Desidirium to make himself the God of Earth. [Subverted](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Subverted "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Subverted"), in that he's really just a [Puppet King](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PuppetKing "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PuppetKing") being used by the two Ranis for their own ends.
*   [Goo-Goo-Godlike](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GooGooGodlike "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GooGooGodlike"): Desidirium is just an infant, but he's powerful enough, albeit with the Vindicator, to reshape the world to Conrad's whims.
*   [Gratuitous Disco Sequence](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GratuitousDiscoSequence "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GratuitousDiscoSequence"): A variation in the climax. While the Rani leads the Doctor in a traditional waltz, the dancing is also beneath an activated disco ball.
*   [Heroic BSoD](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicBSOD "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicBSOD"): The Doctor is shaken by the revelation that his life with a wife isn't what it seems. After his talk with Rogue, he feverishly demonstrates to Belinda that tables really don't work this way. When the fake reality further breaks inside the Ranis' palace, he collapses to the ground, clutching his head.
*   [Horrifying the Horror](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HorrifyingTheHorror "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HorrifyingTheHorror"): Godly powers aside, Desidirium is an ordinary baby. He still terrifies the spit out of Mrs. Flood and Conrad.
*   [Innocently Insensitive](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InnocentlyInsensitive "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InnocentlyInsensitive"): Ruby asks Brian whether he figured Conrad was evil from the sound of his voice. He ribs her for assuming he has magic powers because he's blind, an accusation she takes in relative stride.
*   [Interrupted Declaration of Love](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InterruptedDeclarationOfLove "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InterruptedDeclarationOfLove"): Rogue is about to tell the Doctor he loves him when the signal from the Underverse is cut off.
*   [Just a Stupid Accent](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JustAStupidAccent "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JustAStupidAccent"): As she collects Desidirium from his parents, the new Rani peppers her speech with accented German words.
*   [Leaning on the Fourth Wall](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LeaningOnTheFourthWall "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LeaningOnTheFourthWall"):
    *   While telling the Doctor about her plans and what she has done to cause the current version of events, the Rani states that what she is saying [isn't just exposition](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LampshadeHanging "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LampshadeHanging"), and is actually a vital part of her plan in order to get the Doctor expressing doubt.
    *   When last we saw the TARDIS, her doors were exploding in. Toward the end of this episode, the Rani taunts the Doctor by asking the same question viewers are probably wondering: What happened to her, and where is she now?
*   [Lotus-Eater Machine](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LotusEaterMachine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LotusEaterMachine"): The world Conrad has created using Desidirium's powers puts people in a state of perpetual bliss, with any doubts or questioning it's societal norms seen as disruptive to their happiness. This does not stop them from doubting those norms or questioning the whole state of reality, but unlike many examples of this trope, this is actually part of the Rani's plan.
*   [Magical Seventh Son](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MagicalSeventhSon "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MagicalSeventhSon"): Desidirium, the infant God of Wishes, is born to the seventh son of a seventh son, and he has six brothers of his own.
*   [Meaningful Echo](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MeaningfulEcho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MeaningfulEcho"): Conrad is, not surprisingly, nursing a grudge over the Doctor calling him "nothing", and takes the time to throw it back in his face, even though at that moment the Doctor doesn't have any memory of doing it.
*   [Memory Trigger](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MemoryTrigger "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MemoryTrigger"): The Doctor's memories fully return when the new Rani mentions Omega.
*   [Nightmare of Normality](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NightmareOfNormality "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NightmareOfNormality"): Conrad's wish forces the Doctor, a gay man, and Belinda into a fantasy of the heteronormative mid-20th century nuclear family. Also, disabled people are literally invisible in the eyes of the non-disabled.
*   [Not Quite Dead](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NotQuiteDead "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/NotQuiteDead"): Rogue's [Heroic Sacrifice](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSacrifice "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicSacrifice") didn't result in his death. From the Underverse, he transmits a warning to the Doctor about Conrad's reality.
*   [Ominous Visual Glitch](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OminousVisualGlitch "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OminousVisualGlitch"): [Downplayed](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DownplayedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DownplayedTrope"). Whenever someone doubts Conrad's reality, and there's a table nearby with a cup on it, the cup falls through, breaking upon impact with the floor. Rogue's note that tables don't work this way is the first hint to the Doctor that something's wrong.
*   [Other Me Annoys Me](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OtherMeAnnoysMe "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OtherMeAnnoysMe"): The Ranis are still this, with Mrs Flood grumbling about how [she's been essentially reduced to Conrad's tea lady](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouGetMeCoffee "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouGetMeCoffee"), and taking great glee in annoying the current Rani when she gets the chance.
*   [Outdated Outfit](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OutdatedOutfit "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OutdatedOutfit"): The circumstances of the wish world mean that there's some zig-zagging in this regard. It's 2025, so the outfits worn by Ruby and the residents of Shirley's camp shouldn't be out of place… yet because Conrad wanted a 60s-ish aesthetic, they're decades from being fashionable.
*   [Parental Abandonment](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ParentalAbandonment "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ParentalAbandonment"): Ruby's mother calls the police on her for doubting, leaving Ruby homeless.
*   [Pet the Dog](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PetTheDog "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PetTheDog"): Amazingly, given absolutely everything else about him, Conrad actually seems polite towards Mrs. Flood and hugs her. It likely helps that she's a pseudo-maternal figure who encourages and comforts him, unlike his own mother.
*   [Puppet King](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PuppetKing "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PuppetKing"): For all Conrad's [A God Am I](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGodAmI "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AGodAmI") boasts to the Doctor, it's clear to the viewer that he's actually swapped one prison for another. Especially once it turns out the whole point of the scenario is that he _can't_ maintain it.
*   [Reality-Breaking Paradox](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityBreakingParadox "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityBreakingParadox"): This is [exploited](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ExploitedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ExploitedTrope") by the Ranis in their quest to break Omega out of the Underverse. They know people will question Conrad's reality, especially when they're [warned not to](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BriarPatching "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BriarPatching"), and through this, they slowly gather the energy required to open a portal into the Underverse. The remainder is provided by the Doctor's [Heroic BSoD](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicBSOD "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeroicBSOD"), something eagerly anticipated by the new Rani.
*   [Reality Is Out to Lunch](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityIsOutToLunch "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityIsOutToLunch"): The entire premise of the episode. The Rani has found the God of Wishes, and is using the Doctor's series-long trek across space and time with the Vindicator to power a reality-warping wish to disrupt the Earth and open a pathway to the Underverse, where Omega has been imprisoned since before the Time War.
*   [Reality Warper](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityWarper "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RealityWarper"): Desidirium, the infant god of wishes, is the one powering the wish world. The Rani actually points out that warping reality on the scale seen in the episode is unsustainable and if enough doubt builds up, it will collapse. Which is exactly what the Rani wants to happen.
*   [Regained Memories Sequence](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RegainedMemoriesSequence "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RegainedMemoriesSequence"): When the new Rani asks the Doctor to name the girl he met (Ruby), he remembers scenes from "[The Church on Ruby Road](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2023CSTheChurchOnRubyRoad "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2023CSTheChurchOnRubyRoad")".
*   [Ripple-Effect-Proof Memory](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RippleEffectProofMemory "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RippleEffectProofMemory"): [Played With](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlayedWith "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlayedWith") throughout the episode. Shirley and a group of other disabled civillians are able to remember the other world better than most everyone else, as does Ruby, which is suggested to be because of her experiences in "[73 Yards](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards")". However, it's eventually revealed that _everybody_ in the wished world is capable of having doubts about their reality and remembering traces of their former lives, and that this is all an intentional part of the Ranis' design.
*   [Rule of Symbolism](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RuleOfSymbolism "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RuleOfSymbolism"): A world based on the mid-20th century ideal, where families are nuclear, most women are housewives, racism is subtle but pervasive, any hint of queerness invites backlash, and disabled and other unwanted people are relegated to the forgotten margins of society... and it's all the fantasy of a blinkered reactionary that's explicitly unsustainable, with the mere act of doubting it literally causing it to collapse in on itself.
*   [Say My Name](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SayMyName "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SayMyName"): The episode ends the Doctor screaming the Ranis' name as he falls into the Underverse.
*   [Self-Proclaimed Liar](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SelfProclaimedLiar "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SelfProclaimedLiar"): In conversation with Conrad, Mrs. Flood asks if she would lie, then backtracks and admits that, yeah, she would. But she's not lying at the moment.
*   [Ship Tease](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShipTease "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShipTease"): The Rani suggests that she and the Doctor were once lovers.
*   [Shipper on Deck](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShipperOnDeck "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ShipperOnDeck"): John Smith encourages Ibrahim to ask Kate to dinner, possibly at a Chinese restaurant. His encouragement takes on a darker tone with the indication that if Ibrahim and Kate got together, she'd eventually be forced to stop working.
*   [Soul-Crushing Desk Job](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SoulCrushingDeskJob "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SoulCrushingDeskJob"): In Conrad's world, UNIT is an insurance company, which John Smith works at.
*   [Speak in Unison](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpeakInUnison "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpeakInUnison"): The two Ranis do this when they tell John they're both Ranis.
*   [Spot the Thread](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpotTheThread "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpotTheThread"): Rogue tries to free the Doctor from the power of Conrad's wish world by bringing up how the tables there don't work the way they should do, hoping that it would give the Doctor enough doubt to begin to unravel the whole thing.
*   [Stay in the Kitchen](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StayInTheKitchen "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StayInTheKitchen"): In Conrad's rewritten reality, women are expected to be wives and mothers and nothing more. John Smith expects that Kate would have to stop working if she and Ibhrahim became romantically involved.
*   [Stock Audio Clip](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StockAudioClip "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/StockAudioClip"): Omega's lines at the very end are uplifted from "Intervention Earth", one of the stories from the [Big Finish](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/BigFinish "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/BigFinish") range _[Gallifrey](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/AudioPlay/Gallifrey "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/AudioPlay/Gallifrey")_.
*   [The Stool Pigeon](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheStoolPigeon "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheStoolPigeon"): Ruby was reported by Carla for doubting the wish world. It's not made clear whether she was arrested.
*   [Trojan Horse](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TrojanHorse "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TrojanHorse"): The Vindicator is revealed to have been this. What the Doctor thought was a way to get Belinda home has actually been gathering power for the Ranis' plan, amplifying Conrad's wish on Desidirium so that it covers the entire world.
*   [The Un-Reveal](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheUnreveal "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheUnreveal"): What did happen to the TARDIS? The Rani brings it up, implying she knows, but doesn't tell the Doctor.
*   [Unusually Uninteresting Sight](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/UnusuallyUninterestingSight "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/UnusuallyUninterestingSight"): A number of titanic skeletal quadrupeds are walking around London in Conrad's world, and absolutely no one seems to so much as notice how out of place they are. Justified, since doubt is forbidden.
*   [Wham Line](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamLine"):
    *   As reality falls around them, the Doctor asks in panic whom the Rani is looking for beneath the Underverse. Her response is short, simple and _anything_ but sweet:
    *   In the final seconds of the episode, the Doctor shouts this in anguish as he falls into the holes in the world. Keep in mind that he's snapped out of his false reality at this point:
*   [Wham Sound](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamSound "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhamSound"): When Conrad picks up the baby, it laughs with the Giggle used by members of the Pantheon.
*   [What the Hell, Hero?](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhatTheHellHero "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WhatTheHellHero"): [Downplayed](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DownplayedTrope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DownplayedTrope"), and [Played for Laughs](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlayedForLaughs "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlayedForLaughs"). In his message to the Doctor, Rogue sarcastically thanks him for being banished to the Underverse.
*   [World-Wrecking Wave](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldWreckingWave "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldWreckingWave"): Once the Doctor's doubts reach their limit, the fabric of reality across London starts to fall apart.
*   [Would Hurt a Child](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WouldHurtAChild "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WouldHurtAChild"): The Rani turns Desidirium's brothers into ducks.
*   [You Can't Thwart Stage One](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouCantThwartStageOne "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/YouCantThwartStageOne"): The Rani has been following the Doctor and his vindicator across time and space so she can use it to boost the power of a baby god to rewrite the world to Conrad's desires, just so the Doctor's doubt can destroy it and drag everything into the Underverse. And _then_ she can start her actual plan.

* * *

by [Simon Brew](https://filmstories.co.uk/author/simon) | May 24, 2025

**Wish World! It’s the best Rani episode of all time. Here’s our spoiler-filled review of Doctor Who season 2’s penultimate episode.**

* * *

_This review contains spoilers. Our review of last week’s episode is [here](https://filmstories.co.uk/tv/the-interstellar-song-contest/)._

They don’t require poster quotes for episodes of _Doctor Who_, but if they did, I’m going to start with one: _Wish World_ is the best Rani episode in the history of the series. In terms of what’s required to get over that bar, it’s less a leap and more a slight lifting of the leg. But still: I stand by my words.

In fact, there’s much to like in _Wish World_, in what increasingly looks like the penultimate episode of _Doctor Who_ for the forseeable future. It arrives on screens at a point where [speculation has ignited again](https://deadline.com/2025/05/doctor-who-ratings-drop-speculation-future-1236409467/) about _Doctor Who_ beyond next week, and yet while all the noise is going on, the show itself has been on a really confident streak.

In the case of _Wish World_, it’s a bubbling to the top of the simmering rage underpinning the writing of season two.

Sure, the usual suspects are writing all this off as ‘woke’ (some of whom occasionally going as far as to look up what the word means), but I’m going with the word angry. Take the reappearance of Conrad, who was introduced back in _Lucky Day_, itself an episode assumed to be a precursor to upcoming spin-off show _The War Between The Land And The Sea_. Rescued from a police cell by Anita Dobson’s Mrs Flood, he’s now, we learn, the creator of the world as he sees it. An angry man on the internet who finally gets his way, and his desire is a world where women are in the kitchen, men wear bowler hats and go to work.

Things then pick up in the aftermath of last week’s _The Interstellar Song Contest_, with two Ranis, one of whom is in 1865 Bavaria. Note the significance of a baby being born that’s of particular interest to Archie Punjabi’s Rani. A lot of talk of seventh son of seventh sons there, before she starts turning people into ducks, flowers and owls.

Post-opening credits, Russell T Davies is having fun. I’ve never seen an intimacy coordinator listed in the end credits of _Doctor Who_ before, but suddenly, the Doctor and Belinda are in matching nightwear, husband and wife. We’re left wondering where the hell are we, as the production design takes another terrific leap. But it becomes clear that a story is being told.

If J K Rowling happened to be tuning in, she surely can’t fail to have noticed that the story being read by an extreme influencer on the internet bears a very striking resemblance to the front of a Harry Potter tome. Surely a coincidence, that. The narrator of said book is our old chum Conrad, and the first half of the episode was both unexpected and really good fun. A lot of smashed mugs, and a lot of pastel colours.

Old _Who_ fans might remember the classic Jon Pertwee story _Inferno_, where the regular characters could basically swap roles for a bit (it’s bloody brilliant if you’ve not seen it: [you can find it on iPlayer here](https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/p00v78k6/doctor-who-19631996-season-7-inferno-episode-1)). I got a sense of that here, just crossed with The Wicked Witch Of The West on her broomstick, a massive clock that looked like it’d been shipped in from a luxurious production of _Alice In Wonderland_, and then something a bit _Stepford Wives_ about the apparent perfection of the world we’re presented with.

The key to unlocking this world proves to be Millie Gibson’s Ruby Sunday, who seven episodes into this series, feels like she’s had a more pivotal role than either the Doctor or Belinda. And she’s only been in two episodes. Still, stepping through that lovely production design and those broken mugs, we’re actually where the Doctor and Bel have been trying to get to, it’s just gone a bit _Back To The Future Part II_ alternative world. Albeit with a massive dinosaur fossil rampaging through. That vortex vindicator thing didn’t quite have the intended effect.

![Image 6: Doctor Who Conrad reading a book](https://spaces.filmstories.co.uk/uploads/2025/05/Doctor-Who-Conrad-reading-a-book-800x451.jpg)

For those who’ve been following the show, meanwhile, there are links to other episodes all over the shop. Back in my Den Of Geek days, we had a fine chap called Pete Dillon-Trenchard – hello Pete! – who wrote extensively about the cross-references to be found in episodes. A field day would be had here.

Might that, then, be the storytelling nexus thingy from _The Story & The Engine_ in there? Look! There’s all of UNIT, just with a new name, and some of them without a job (note the point about people walking past other people on the street). Susan Triad, she’s back from the last series, and she’s au fait with The Rani. Oooh, there’s Mel as well. Wasn’t it said that she’d gone off to Sydney recently? Now, here she is in alternate world, with impeccable recycling.

Then! With the talk of a tiny baby who sustains the entire world, I did have an oh-my-lord are we really going back to _Space Babies_ moment.

Hang on, though! What does the Doctor call himself in his new life? John Smith. We’ve been here before, and not just when we fancy a trip to the off licence. David Tennant’s Doctor lived a happy life as John Smith back in _The Family Of Blood_ two-parter, before finding his real self unlocked by a watch. No such watch was required to get memories back here, but I swear Murray Gold put a tiny bit of The Master’s score in the music to this episode. I found myself half-expecting The Rani to wheel him out, what with the hints as to the greater force.

But no! Our tour through _Doctor Who_ past has led us, seemingly, to the door of Omega, the creator of the Time Lords. Heck, I remember the fuss just over his hand in _Remembrance Of The Daleks_. Elsewhere in Omega-world, I still think you need a degree to unlock _Arc Of Infinity_, but more recently, Chris Chibnall brought him back in _The Timeless Children_. Is Russell T Davies really going to have a go, or is he doing a bit of misdirection?

![Image 7: Doctor Who Wish World](https://spaces.filmstories.co.uk/uploads/2025/05/Doctor-Who-Wish-World-image-800x533.jpg)

He certainly seems pissed off. If the ultimate overarching threat of season two proves to be Conrad, his beliefs, and how he thinks the world should be run, then Davies has taken a long hard stare at the world, and responded in kind. A modern-day thought police keeping the people of a world in check, stopping them speaking out about the extremist who holds them in their place? That’s actually chilling, primarily because it doesn’t feel that fictional.

And then on top of all of this was an outpouring of visuals that kicked in throughout the second half of the episode, as the destruction and collapse of things took hold. In fact, in the midst of all the references and reappearances was a standard, entertaining penultimate episodes, with one of those cliffhangers that looks to be easily resolved, basically the world falling apart.

The key to saving the universe this time might just be with Mrs Flood, already showing a tiny bit of frustration at her counterpart bossing her around. And here, I found Anita Dobson really quite unnerving. If Archie Punjabi is channelling a bit of John Simm’s Master in her portrayal of The Rani, Dobson has gone the other way and found a far creepier register.

Note too that Susan didn’t reappear this week. Surely she’s going to pop up next.

The other one to keep an eye on is baby Poppy, but also, it’s likely to be all hands on deck for _The Reality War_ next week, an episode that increasingly looks like being the final _Doctor Who_ instalment for quite a while. I know the usual outlets like kicking this show about, and I know _Doctor Who_ has made its fair share of miss-steps. But I’ve really enjoyed this season, and when all the grown-ups and tabloids have finished telling the kids how woke and terrible it is, a whole bunch of us – young and old – are having a great time.

_Wish World_? Enjoyable, scene-setting, over-the-top, bombastic, angry, a little bit having its cake and eating it. Far more entertaining that reading a copy of The Sun.

And, to date, the best Rani episode of all time.
